intro: Dynamic programming (DP) solves problems that exhibit optimal substructure (an optimal solution can be built from optimal solutions to subproblems) and overlapping subproblems (the same subproblem recurs many times during a naive recursive solution). Instead of recomputing shared subproblems exponentially many times, DP either memoizes them (caches results of a top-down recursion) or tabulates them (fills a bottom-up table in an order that respects dependencies), reducing runtime from exponential to polynomial. The entire skill of DP is: define a state precisely enough that it captures everything future decisions depend on, write a correct recurrence (transition) between states, and get the base cases and evaluation order right — everything below is a set of recognizable patterns for doing that.

subtopics.name: DP Fundamentals
subtopics.theory:
Every DP solution rests on three ingredients: a **state** (a tuple of parameters that fully describes a subproblem), a **transition/recurrence** (how a state's answer is computed from smaller/earlier states), and **base cases** (the smallest subproblems solved directly, without recursion). A recursive brute force becomes DP the moment you notice the recursion tree revisits identical (state) calls repeatedly — overlapping subproblems. Two implementation strategies compute the same recurrence: memoization (top-down) writes the recursion exactly as you'd think of it recursively, and wraps it in a cache (array or hash map) so each distinct state is computed once; tabulation (bottom-up) instead iterates over states in an order guaranteeing every state's dependencies are already filled in, storing answers in a table (usually an array).

Memoization is easier to derive correctly (you write the natural recursion and add a cache check at the top and a cache write before every return) and it only computes states that are actually reachable from the initial call, which matters when the full state space is large but the reachable subset is small. Tabulation is usually faster in practice (no recursion/function-call overhead, better cache locality) and makes space optimization straightforward — if dp[i] only depends on dp[i-1] and dp[i-2], you can drop the array to O(1) rolling variables, something far more awkward to see through a memoized recursion. The two are mechanically interchangeable: any tabulated DP can be rewritten top-down and vice versa, so in practice you pick whichever is easier to reason about for the recurrence at hand, then switch to the other if you hit its weaknesses (stack depth for memoization on deep recursion, unreachable-state waste for tabulation).

A state definition is correct if and only if it satisfies the **Markov / optimal-substructure property**: the best way to complete a state depends only on the state itself, not on how you arrived there. If two different histories reach 'the same' state but require different future decisions, the state is under-specified and must be enlarged (this is exactly what upgrades naive greedy attempts into DP with extra dimensions).
subtopics.recognition: Suspect DP when a problem asks for an optimum (min/max), a count of ways, or a yes/no feasibility over a search space that is exponential if you tried all possibilities directly, AND you can describe a smaller version of the same problem that a full solution decomposes into (i.e., 'the answer for n depends on the answer for some smaller n''). If greedy 'obviously' fails on some case, or brute-force recursion clearly repeats identical subcalls, that's a strong DP signal.
subtopics.complexity: Complexity is (number of distinct states) x (work per transition). Memoization and tabulation have identical asymptotic complexity for the same recurrence; tabulation usually has a smaller constant factor and enables O(states) -> O(1)-per-layer space optimization via rolling arrays when the recurrence only reaches back a bounded number of previous layers.

examples.title: Coin Change — Minimum Coins (Bottom-Up Tabulation)
examples.problem:
You are given n coin denominations and a target amount. Determine the minimum number of coins (unlimited supply of each denomination) needed to make exactly that amount, or report -1 if it is impossible.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 100, 1 <= coin value <= 10^4, 0 <= amount <= 10^4.
examples.approach: Define dp[x] = minimum coins to make amount x, with dp[0] = 0 as the base case (zero coins needed for zero amount). For every amount x from 1 up to the target, and for every coin c <= x, dp[x] = min(dp[x], dp[x - c] + 1) — you are trying 'what if the last coin used was c', and the rest (x - c) is a strictly smaller subproblem already solved because we iterate x in increasing order (bottom-up tabulation). Initialize all dp entries to infinity except dp[0]; if dp[amount] is still infinity at the end, it is unreachable, so print -1. This is the unbounded-knapsack recurrence (each coin may be reused, which is exactly why the inner loop iterates coins for a fixed x rather than the other way around with a descending sweep, the way bounded 0/1 knapsack requires).

examples.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence Length (Top-Down Memoization)
examples.problem:
Given an array of n integers, find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (elements need not be contiguous).
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 2500.
examples.approach: Define lis(i) = length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence that ends exactly at index i. The recurrence is lis(i) = 1 + max(lis(j)) over all j < i with a[j] < a[i], or just 1 if no such j exists (the subsequence containing only a[i]). Written as a plain recursive function this naturally calls lis(j) for every j < i, and the same lis(j) gets requested again for every larger i — classic overlapping subproblems — so we memoize with an array memo[i] initialized to -1 (uncomputed). The final answer is max(lis(i)) over all i, since the longest increasing subsequence can end anywhere. This is the O(n^2) DP (as opposed to the O(n log n) patience-sorting method), presented top-down to contrast with the bottom-up tabulation used in the coin-change example above — note it computes lis(i) purely from smaller indices, so the memoized recursion never needs to worry about cyclic dependencies.

subtopics.name: Linear/1D DP
subtopics.theory:
Linear DP indexes the state by a single position (usually 'considering the first i elements' or 'the subsequence ending at i') and the transition looks back at a bounded or unbounded number of earlier positions. The hallmark is a state array dp[i] (possibly with a small number of extra dimensions bolted on for auxiliary constraints — how many items used, how much capacity spent, etc.) where the recurrence dp[i] = f(dp[i-1], dp[i-2], ..., dp[0]) is evaluated left to right (or right to left).

Two recurring sub-patterns dominate this category. First, 'take or skip' recurrences (house-robber style) where dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + value[i]) — the decision at each position is binary and only depends on a fixed lookback window, so these are O(n) and trivially space-optimizable to O(1). Second, 'best subsequence ending here' recurrences (LIS-style) where dp[i] depends on ALL previous j < i satisfying some compatibility predicate, giving a naive O(n^2); when the predicate is monotonic (strictly increasing values, or non-overlapping time intervals), the search over j can be accelerated to O(log n) with binary search, a Fenwick/BIT tree, or a monotonic structure that tracks the best dp value seen so far for each possible 'key'.

A third, more advanced sub-pattern compresses an exponential search over subsets/orderings into a linear DP by using a bitmask as part of the state (dp[mask] or dp[mask][last]) — this only scales to n around 15-22 since the state space is 2^n, but it turns NP-hard-looking combinatorial search (visit every city / person / row exactly once) into a polynomial-in-2^n DP, which is the standard trick for small-n exact combinatorial optimization.
subtopics.recognition: Look for: 'array/sequence, choose a subsequence or a schedule of non-overlapping items to optimize a sum', 'longest / shortest chain where each element can only follow certain predecessors', or 'n is tiny (<=20) and the problem talks about visiting every item/city/person exactly once' (bitmask DP). The state is naturally 1D (plus maybe a bounded number of extra scalar dimensions), and the recurrence looks backward along the sequence, not across two independent dimensions like a grid.
subtopics.complexity: Take-or-skip DP: O(n) time, O(1) space after rolling-array optimization. Naive 'ending at i' DP: O(n^2) time, O(n) space; with binary search / BIT acceleration: O(n log n) time. Bitmask DP over subsets: O(2^n * n) or O(2^n * n^2) time, O(2^n) space — only tractable for n up to about 20.

examples.title: Maximum Profit in Job Scheduling (Weighted Interval Scheduling)
examples.problem:
You are given n jobs, each with a start time, end time, and profit. A job occupies [start, end]; two jobs may be scheduled together only if one ends at or before the other starts (touching endpoints are allowed). Choose a subset of non-overlapping jobs maximizing total profit.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 5*10^4, 1 <= start < end <= 10^9, 1 <= profit <= 10^4.
examples.approach: Sort jobs by end time. Let dp[i] = the maximum profit achievable using only the first i jobs in this sorted order (job i itself is optional). For the i-th job (1-indexed after sorting) with (s, e, p): either skip it, giving dp[i-1], or take it, giving p plus the best profit obtainable from jobs that finish at or before s. Because jobs are sorted by end time, 'jobs finishing at or before s' is a prefix of the sorted list, so its boundary can be located with binary search (upper_bound on the array of sorted end times) rather than a linear scan, giving dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[k] + p) where k is the count of earlier jobs ending at or before s. dp[0] = 0 is the base case (no jobs used). The final answer is dp[n].

examples.title: Super Egg Drop
examples.problem:
You are given k identical eggs and a building with n floors. An egg breaks if dropped from at or above some unknown critical floor f (0 <= f <= n; f = 0 means even floor 1 breaks it), and survives if dropped below f. A broken egg cannot be reused; a surviving egg can be reused. Determine the minimum number of moves needed, in the worst case, to determine f exactly.
Constraints: 1 <= k <= 100, 1 <= n <= 10^4.
examples.approach: The natural DP dp[moves][eggs] = 'worst-case floors resolvable' would need an inner search over which floor to drop from first, giving O(k n^2) or O(k n log n) — workable but not the cleanest. The key reformulation: instead of asking 'how many moves to solve n floors with k eggs', ask f(t, k) = 'the maximum number of floors distinguishable using at most t moves and k eggs'. Dropping an egg from some floor either breaks it (reducing to f(t-1, k-1) floors above) or survives (reducing to f(t-1, k) floors below), plus the floor you just tested itself, so f(t, k) = f(t-1, k-1) + f(t-1, k) + 1, with base cases f(t, 0) = 0 and f(0, k) = 0. This DP is monotone increasing in t, so the answer is the smallest t with f(t, k) >= n — found by simply incrementing t and filling one new row of the table at a time until the threshold is reached. Because f(t, 1) = t, t never needs to exceed n, bounding the loop.

examples.title: Russian Doll Envelopes (2D LIS)
examples.problem:
Given n envelopes as (width, height) pairs, find the maximum number that can be nested inside one another, where envelope A fits inside envelope B only if both A.width < B.width and A.height < B.height (strict on both dimensions).
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 10^5, 1 <= width, height <= 10^5.
examples.approach: Sort envelopes by width ascending; to correctly forbid nesting two envelopes of equal width inside each other, break width ties by sorting height descending. After this sort, the problem reduces exactly to finding the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of the height sequence: because widths are non-decreasing left to right and equal-width groups have their heights in decreasing order, any strictly increasing run of heights automatically comes from strictly increasing widths too (equal-width envelopes can never both appear in an increasing height run, since within a tie group heights only decrease). Solve this reduced LIS with the O(n log n) patience-sorting technique: maintain an array 'tails' where tails[len-1] is the smallest possible tail value of an increasing subsequence of length len; for each height, binary search (lower_bound) for where it belongs and either extend or replace.

subtopics.name: 2D Grid DP
subtopics.theory:
Grid DP states are indexed by a cell position (r, c), with the recurrence moving in the grid's allowed directions (usually right/down for monotone-path problems). The default pattern — count paths, or find min/max cost path from top-left to bottom-right — sets dp[r][c] = f(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1]) and fills the table in reading order (row by row, left to right), since both dependencies come from earlier rows/columns.

A subtler but common twist is that the natural forward direction of the DP produces an ill-defined state. Dungeon Game is the canonical example: if you try to track 'maximum health after reaching (r,c)' forward from the top-left, the greedy-looking 'maximize health so far' choice at each step is not actually optimal, because a path that arrives with more health now might need more health later for a bad room ahead — the state needs future information the forward direction doesn't have yet. The fix is to run the DP backward from the destination, where dp[r][c] = 'minimum health needed upon entering (r,c) to survive optimally from here to the end' — now the recurrence only needs already-solved future cells, and it's well-defined.

When a problem needs multiple simultaneous agents traversing the grid (two robots, or one round trip modeled as two forward walkers), the state grows to include every agent's position, constrained so all agents take the same number of steps at once — e.g. dp[step][r1][c1... but c2 derivable][col2] for two robots moving down together. This keeps the DP polynomial (state space is roughly rows * cols^(number of agents)) instead of exponential, as long as the number of agents stays small (2, occasionally 3).
subtopics.recognition: Any problem phrased over a 2D grid/matrix with directional movement (right/down, or 4-directional with a visiting constraint) that asks for a count, min/max cost, or feasibility of a path is grid DP. If the state 'as read forward' would need to know something about the future (a min-health / survivability constraint), that's the signal to reverse the DP direction. If multiple tokens/robots move through the grid at once, that's the signal to add extra position dimensions to the state (multi-agent grid DP).
subtopics.complexity: Single-agent monotone-path DP: O(rows * cols) time and space, often O(cols) with a rolling row. Two-agent DP (state = row, col1, col2): O(rows * cols^2) time and space. Hamiltonian-path-style grid problems requiring 4-directional movement that visits every cell exactly once generally need bitmask-augmented search, O(2^(rows*cols) * rows*cols) in the worst case, only tractable when rows*cols is small (<= ~20).

examples.title: Dungeon Game (Reverse-Direction Grid DP)
examples.problem:
A knight starts at the top-left cell of an m x n dungeon and must reach the bottom-right cell, moving only right or down at each step. Each cell has an integer value: negative means the knight loses that much health entering it, positive means the knight gains that much health. The knight's health must remain strictly above 0 at every point along the path (including the very first cell). Find the minimum initial health needed to guarantee survival to the end.
Constraints: 1 <= m, n <= 200, -1000 <= cell value <= 1000.
examples.approach: Define dp[r][c] as the minimum health required upon ENTERING cell (r,c) so that the knight can survive optimally all the way to the bottom-right corner. This must be computed backward, starting from the destination: dp[m-1][n-1] = max(1, 1 - grid[m-1][n-1]) (need at least 1 health after applying that cell's effect, and at least 1 overall). For any other cell, the knight will move to whichever of the right/down neighbor needs less incoming health, so dp[r][c] = max(1, min(dp[r+1][c], dp[r][c+1]) - grid[r][c]) (cells on the last row/column only have one neighbor). The answer is dp[0][0]. Computing forward from the start does not work because 'maximum health accumulated so far' is not a valid state — a path arriving with more current health can still be worse overall if it is about to walk into a large negative cell that a different, lower-health path would have avoided.

examples.title: Cherry Pickup II (Two Robots, Multi-Agent Grid DP)
examples.problem:
Given a grid with `rows` rows and `cols` columns of non-negative cherry counts, robot 1 starts at the top-left cell (0,0) and robot 2 starts at the top-right cell (0, cols-1). Every step, both robots move simultaneously to the next row, each independently choosing to shift one column left, stay, or shift one column right (staying in bounds). Both robots collect the cherries on the cells they land on; if both robots land on the same cell, its cherries are only collected once. Maximize the total cherries collected after both robots reach the last row.
Constraints: 2 <= rows, cols <= 70.
examples.approach: State: dp[r][c1][c2] = maximum cherries collectible from row r onward, given robot 1 is at column c1 and robot 2 is at column c2 in row r. Base case, the last row: dp[rows-1][c1][c2] = grid[rows-1][c1] + (c1 != c2 ? grid[rows-1][c2] : 0). For earlier rows, both robots simultaneously choose one of 3 moves each (9 combinations), so dp[r][c1][c2] = grid[r][c1] + (c1 != c2 ? grid[r][c2] : 0) + max over the 9 valid (c1+d1, c2+d2) combinations of dp[r+1][c1+d1][c2+d2], with d1, d2 in {-1,0,1} and bounds-checked. This is filled bottom-up from the last row upward. The answer is dp[0][0][cols-1], the robots' starting positions.

examples.title: Unique Paths III (Hamiltonian Path Counting via Bitmask DP)
examples.problem:
Given an m x n grid where each cell is 1 (the single start), 2 (the single end), 0 (walkable empty), or -1 (obstacle), count the number of distinct paths from start to end that move up/down/left/right and visit every non-obstacle cell exactly once (including start and end).
Constraints: 1 <= m, n <= 20, m*n <= 20 (small enough for a bitmask state).
examples.approach: Because the total number of non-obstacle cells is at most 20, the set of already-visited cells fits in a bitmask. Define a search dfs(r, c, mask) = number of ways to complete the tour to the end cell, given the current position is (r,c) and mask records every cell visited so far (including (r,c) itself). If (r,c) is the end cell, the path is only valid if mask has visited every free cell (popcount(mask) == total free cells) — return 1 if so, else 0. Otherwise, try all 4 neighbors that are in bounds, not an obstacle, and not already set in mask, recursing with the bit for that neighbor added. Crucially, the future count from (r,c,mask) depends only on the current position and which cells remain available — not on the order in which they were visited — so (r,c,mask) can be safely memoized, turning an otherwise exponential backtracking search into a bitmask DP over at most (m*n) * 2^(m*n) states.

subtopics.name: Knapsack Family
subtopics.theory:
All knapsack problems share a state of the form dp[items considered][resource used] = best value achievable, and the defining choice at each item is binary: take it or don't. The crucial implementation detail is whether an item can be reused: for 0/1 knapsack (each item at most once), the resource dimension must be iterated in DECREASING order when updating in place (or a fresh row per item must be used), so that an item's own contribution isn't accidentally applied twice; for unbounded knapsack (unlimited copies of each item, as in Coin Change), the resource dimension is iterated in INCREASING order, deliberately allowing dp[x-w] to already reflect having used this same item.

Beyond the textbook 'maximize value subject to a weight limit' framing, the real skill tested in hard knapsack problems is recognizing which quantity should be the tracked resource dimension when it is not obviously a weight. Sometimes it's a count of items used (Profitable Schemes: members used x profit achieved, with the profit axis clamped at the target so the state space stays polynomial). Sometimes the natural target isn't a sum you can pin down in advance but a running SIGNED DIFFERENCE between two groups (Tallest Billboard: index by height-difference, often via a hash map since the difference can be negative or sparse). Sometimes what you're really doing is bin-packing in disguise, where the 'capacity' resets across multiple knapsacks (bins/rides) and the cleanest state is a bitmask over which items are already packed, together with how much room is left in the current bin (Elevator Rides) — this only scales to item counts of about 20 or fewer, since it's the subset-based, not sum-based, formulation.

Counting variants (how many subsets achieve exactly/at least some target) use the exact same take-or-skip recurrence structure, just summing counts instead of taking a max, and commonly require a modulus and care around double-counting symmetric solutions (e.g. a set and its complement being the 'same' partition).
subtopics.recognition: Suspect knapsack whenever a problem gives a list of items each with one or more costs and asks you to choose a subset under a budget/limit to optimize (or count subsets achieving) some target. If items are reusable, it's unbounded knapsack; if each is used at most once, 0/1. If the 'capacity' resets across multiple containers (rides, trucks, days), think bin-packing via bitmask DP over small n. If the natural resource axis isn't a plain sum but a difference or a count that needs capping, that's a sign the state needs a non-obvious second dimension.
subtopics.complexity: 0/1 and unbounded knapsack: O(n * capacity) time, O(capacity) space with a 1D rolling array (2D-looking value/weight problems become O(n * dim1 * dim2)). Bitmask bin-packing DP: O(2^n * n) time and O(2^n) space, only tractable for n <= ~20. Difference-indexed knapsack (hash-map state): O(n * distinct-difference-values) rather than O(n * sum), which is the whole point when sums are too large to index directly but differences are sparse.

examples.title: Two Sets II — Count Equal-Sum Partitions (Subset-Sum Counting)
examples.problem:
Given n, count the number of ways to partition the set {1, 2, ..., n} into two subsets with equal sums, modulo 10^9+7. (If the total sum of 1..n is odd, the answer is 0.)
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 500.
examples.approach: Let S = n(n+1)/2. If S is odd, no equal split exists, so the answer is 0. Otherwise the target for one side is T = S/2, and we need the number of subsets of {1,...,n} summing exactly to T — a classic 0/1 knapsack counting DP: dp[0] = 1 (the empty subset sums to 0), and for each value i from 1 to n, iterate the sum s from T DOWN to i, doing dp[s] += dp[s-i] (decreasing order is essential so each i is only used once per subset). After processing all n values, dp[T] counts every subset summing to T; each such subset A and its complement (which also sums to T, since the total is 2T) form the same unordered partition into two sets, and A can never equal its own complement (they're disjoint and both non-empty for n >= 1), so dividing dp[T] by 2 (via the modular inverse of 2, since the modulus is an odd prime) gives the number of unordered partitions.

examples.title: Elevator Rides (Bitmask Bin-Packing DP)
examples.problem:
There are n people with given weights and an elevator with a maximum weight capacity x (every person's weight individually fits, weight[i] <= x). Find the minimum number of elevator rides needed to move every person up, where each ride carries any subset of the remaining people whose total weight does not exceed x.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 20.
examples.approach: This is bin-packing: minimize the number of bins (rides) of capacity x. With n <= 20, track a bitmask of which people have already been transported. For each mask, store the Pareto-optimal pair (rides used so far, capacity remaining in the current/last ride), preferring fewer rides, and among equal ride counts, more remaining capacity. Base case dp[empty mask] = (1 ride started, x capacity available, nobody boarded yet). To compute dp[mask], pick any person i in mask, look at dp[mask without i] = (r, cap): if person i's weight fits in the remaining capacity cap, they join the current ride, giving (r, cap - weight[i]); otherwise they need a new ride, giving (r+1, x - weight[i]). Take the best candidate over all choices of i (any valid i gives a correct, though not necessarily optimal, decomposition order, and trying every i and keeping the best guarantees optimality). The answer is the ride count of dp[full mask].

examples.title: Profitable Schemes (2D Bounded Knapsack with Clamped Profit)
examples.problem:
You have G members available. There are n given 'crimes', each requiring group[i] members to execute and yielding profit[i]. A profitable scheme is a subset of crimes whose total member requirement is at most G and whose total profit is at least P. Count the number of profitable schemes, modulo 10^9+7 (the empty scheme counts if P = 0).
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 100, 0 <= G <= 100, 0 <= P <= 100.
examples.approach: This is a 2D 0/1 knapsack: the two resource axes are members used (bounded by G) and profit achieved (bounded below by P, but since profits beyond P are all equally 'sufficient', clamp the tracked profit at min(actual, P) to keep this axis's size at P+1 instead of unboundedly large). Let dp[j][k] = number of subsets of crimes considered so far that use exactly j members and achieve clamped profit exactly k. Base case dp[0][0] = 1 (the empty subset). For each crime (g, p), update in 0/1-knapsack fashion by iterating j from G down to g (so each crime is only counted once per subset), and for every k from 0 to P, add dp[j-g][k] into dp[j][min(P, k+p)]. After processing all crimes, the answer is the sum of dp[j][P] over every j from 0 to G — every subset whose clamped profit reached exactly P has real profit >= P.

subtopics.name: Interval DP
subtopics.theory:
Interval DP states are indexed by a contiguous range [l, r] of a sequence, with dp[l][r] representing the best (or only) way to fully resolve that entire subrange. The recurrence almost always tries every way to split or finish the interval at a 'pivot' k, combining the answers for the two resulting pieces: dp[l][r] = opt_k( dp[l][k] + dp[k+1][r] + cost(l,k,r) ) or similar. Filling order is always by increasing interval LENGTH (start with length-1 or length-2 base cases, then length-3, etc.), never by increasing l or r alone, because dp[l][r] depends on strictly shorter sub-intervals nested inside it.

The single most important insight to internalize is 'think about the LAST event, not the first, within the interval'. In Burst Balloons, trying to fix which balloon is burst FIRST inside [l, r] is a dead end, because after bursting it the two resulting sub-ranges are no longer independent (a balloon that used to be adjacent to something outside [l,r] now might not be). Fixing which balloon is burst LAST inside (l, r), however, means both of its neighbors at that moment are guaranteed to be exactly the boundary balloons l and r (everything else inside is already gone), which is why sentinel 1s are padded at both ends and dp[l][r] represents 'the best score for clearing everything strictly between l and r, with l and r themselves surviving until last'.

A second variant is the MINIMAX interval game: two players alternately take from the ends of a sequence, each maximizing their own score. Here dp[l][r] is 'the best score the player to move can guarantee from the remaining subarray [l,r]', and the recurrence must account for the opponent also playing optimally afterward — typically expressed as dp[l][r] = max(a[l] + (sum(l+1,r) - dp[l+1][r]), a[r] + (sum(l,r-1) - dp[l,r-1])), where 'total remaining minus what the opponent optimally takes' gives what's left for you across all your own future turns. A third variant generalizes the split to more than two pieces (merging k consecutive piles, or 2D rectangle cuts), adding an extra dimension for how many pieces are currently grouped, but the length-order evaluation and pivot-search structure stay the same.
subtopics.recognition: Interval DP shows up whenever a problem repeatedly removes, merges, or partitions a contiguous range of a sequence (or matched bracket/palindrome structure) and asks for an optimal (min cost / max value) way to fully process it, especially when doing an operation on part of the range changes what's adjacent to what outside it (signaling 'think about what happens last', not first). Two-player alternating-turn games on an array's ends are a distinct, recognizable minimax sub-flavor of the same [l,r] state shape.
subtopics.complexity: Standard interval DP (pivot search over 2 pieces): O(n^2) states x O(n) pivot search = O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space. Minimax array-game DP: O(n^2) time and space with no extra pivot search (only 2 choices per state). k-way merge / 2D rectangle-cut generalizations: an extra dimension (number of groups, or a second side length) multiplies the state count, typically giving O(n^3 k) or O(a^2 b^2) time.

examples.title: Burst Balloons (Think About the Last Balloon, Not the First)
examples.problem:
Given n balloons in a row with positive integer values, repeatedly burst one balloon; bursting balloon i earns value[left] * value[i] * value[right], where left and right are the balloons currently adjacent to i (or 1 if i is at either current end). Maximize the total coins collected after bursting all balloons.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 500, 0 <= value <= 100.
examples.approach: Pad the array with a sentinel value 1 at both ends: a[0] = 1, a[n+1] = 1, a[1..n] = the original values. Define dp[l][r] = the maximum coins obtainable from bursting every balloon strictly between indices l and r (exclusive), given a[l] and a[r] are NOT burst as part of this subproblem (they persist as the current boundary). Considering balloon k (l < k < r) as the LAST one burst in this range means that at the moment it's burst, everything else strictly between l and r is already gone, so its neighbors at that moment are guaranteed to be exactly a[l] and a[r]: dp[l][r] = max over k in (l,r) of dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + a[l]*a[k]*a[r]. Base case dp[l][r] = 0 whenever r <= l+1 (no balloons strictly between them). Fill by increasing interval length. The answer is dp[0][n+1].

examples.title: Removal Game (Minimax Interval Game DP)
examples.problem:
Two players alternately remove either the first or the last number from a given list of n numbers; the removed number is added to that player's score. Both players play optimally to maximize their own final score. Compute the maximum score the first player can guarantee.
Constraints: 1 <= n <= 5000, values fit in a 32-bit signed integer.
examples.approach: Define dp[l][r] = the best score the player CURRENTLY TO MOVE can guarantee from the remaining subarray a[l..r]. If that player takes a[l], the rest a[l+1..r] becomes a game where the opponent moves first and (optimally) secures dp[l+1][r]; since the opponent's optimal score plus the current player's eventual score from that same subrange must sum to its total, the current player is left with sum(l+1,r) - dp[l+1][r] from all their own future turns in that range. Symmetric reasoning applies if they take a[r] instead. So dp[l][r] = max(a[l] + (sum(l+1,r) - dp[l+1][r]), a[r] + (sum(l,r-1) - dp[l,r-1])), with base case dp[i][i] = a[i] (only one number left, take it). Precompute prefix sums for O(1) range-sum queries. Fill by increasing interval length; the answer is dp[0][n-1].

examples.title: Rectangle Cutting (2D Interval DP)
examples.problem:
Given an a x b rectangle with integer side lengths, you may repeatedly choose any current rectangle and cut it (horizontally or vertically, at an integer position) into two rectangles with integer sides. Find the minimum number of cuts needed so that every remaining piece is a square.
Constraints: 1 <= a, b <= 500.
examples.approach: Define dp[p][q] = minimum cuts to reduce a p x q rectangle entirely to squares. Base case dp[p][p] = 0 (already a square). Otherwise, one cut must be made first, either vertical (splitting p into i and p-i for some 1 <= i < p, giving two independent sub-rectangles i x q and (p-i) x q) or horizontal (splitting q similarly). subtopics.name: String DP
subtopics.theory:
String DP almost always uses a 2D state dp[i][j] = 'considering the first i characters of string s and the first j characters of string t' (or a single string's substring bounds [i][j] for palindrome-style problems), because comparing or aligning two strings inherently needs two independent position pointers. The transition inspects the characters s[i-1] and t[j-1] (0-indexed strings, 1-indexed DP to cleanly represent 'zero characters used' as index 0) and branches on whether they match, whether one side has a wildcard, or whether a character is inserted/deleted/replaced.

The canonical checkpoint problem is Edit Distance: dp[i][j] = minimum insertions/deletions/substitutions to turn s[0..i) into t[0..j), with dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] when the characters match, or 1 + min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]) (delete from s, insert into s, or substitute) otherwise; base cases dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j. Every harder string-matching DP (wildcard matching, regex matching) is a variation on this same alignment-table shape, with the added complexity of pattern metacharacters creating NON-LOCAL transitions: a '*' meaning 'zero or more of the preceding element' means dp[i][j] can depend not just on dp[i-1][j-1] but on dp[i][j-2] (treat the starred group as matching zero characters, skipping backward over it entirely) as well as dp[i-1][j] (treat it as consuming one more character of s and re-trying the same pattern position). Getting the 'zero occurrences' skip-back case right, without off-by-one errors in the index it skips back to, is the single most common source of bugs in this whole family.

Counting variants (Distinct Subsequences) replace 'min cost' with 'sum of ways': dp[i][j] = number of ways t[0..j) appears as a subsequence of s[0..i) is dp[i-1][j] (don't use s[i-1]) plus dp[i-1][j-1] if s[i-1] == t[j-1] (do use it to match t[j-1]) — a fork that resembles 0/1 knapsack's take-or-skip structure, transplanted onto two strings instead of items and a capacity. Finally, some 'string DP' problems are secretly a different family in disguise: minimum insertions to make a string a palindrome reduces exactly to n minus the longest common subsequence of the string and its reverse, which is worth recognizing rather than re-deriving an interval-DP palindrome recurrence from scratch.
subtopics.recognition: Two strings (or one string compared against itself/its reverse) with a request for minimum edit operations, whether one matches a pattern with wildcards, or a count of ways one appears as a subsequence/transformation of the other, all point to a dp[i][j] 2D alignment table. Pattern metacharacters ('*', '?', '.') are the tell for non-local transitions that need careful 'skip the whole starred group' handling.
subtopics.complexity: O(n*m) time and space for the standard alignment DP, where n, m are the two string lengths; easily reducible to O(min(n,m)) space with a rolling pair of rows since each row only depends on the previous one. Pattern-matching variants with '*' keep the same O(n*m) time/space, just with a slightly larger constant per cell for the extra case analysis.

examples.title: Edit Distance (Canonical 2D Alignment DP)
examples.problem:
Given two strings s and t, find the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to transform s into t.
Constraints: 1 <= |s|, |t| <= 5000, lowercase/uppercase letters.
examples.approach: dp[i][j] = edit distance between s[0..i) and t[0..j). Base cases: dp[0][j] = j (insert all of t's first j characters into an empty s) and dp[i][0] = i (delete all of s's first i characters to reach an empty t). Transition: if s[i-1] == t[j-1], the last characters already match for free, so dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j] (delete s[i-1]), dp[i][j-1] (insert t[j-1]), dp[i-1][j-1] (substitute s[i-1] for t[j-1])). Fill row by row; the answer is dp[n][m].

examples.title: Regular Expression Matching ('.' and '*')
examples.problem:
Given a string s and a pattern p containing lowercase letters, '.' (matches any single character), and '*' (matches zero or more of the preceding element), determine whether p matches the entirety of s. Print "true" or "false". The pattern is guaranteed valid (a '*' is always preceded by a literal character or '.').
Constraints: 1 <= |s| <= 20, 1 <= |p| <= 30.
examples.approach: dp[i][j] = true if s[0..i) matches p[0..j). Base case dp[0][0] = true (empty matches empty). dp[0][j] (matching empty s against a pattern prefix) is only true when p[j-1] is '*' and dp[0][j-2] is true (the starred element can vanish, leaving whatever was true before it). For i,j >= 1: if p[j-1] == '*', two ways to satisfy it: treat the preceding element as matched ZERO times, giving dp[i][j] |= dp[i][j-2] (skip the whole 'element*' group entirely, WITHOUT consuming any of s); or, if the preceding pattern element (p[j-2]) matches s[i-1] (equal, or p[j-2] is '.'), treat it as matched one more time, giving dp[i][j] |= dp[i-1][j] (consume one character of s, stay on the same '*' pattern position since it can repeat). If p[j-1] is a literal or '.' (no following '*'), it must match s[i-1] directly: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] if p[j-1] == '.' or p[j-1] == s[i-1], else false. The answer is dp[n][m].

examples.title: Distinct Subsequences (Counting Alignment DP)
examples.problem:
Given strings s and t, count the number of distinct ways t appears as a subsequence of s (subsequences occurring at different index positions in s count separately even if they produce the same characters).
Constraints: 1 <= |s| <= 1000, 1 <= |t| <= 1000.
examples.approach: dp[i][j] = number of ways t[0..j) is a subsequence of s[0..i). Base cases: dp[i][0] = 1 for every i (the empty string is a subsequence of anything in exactly one way — pick nothing), and dp[0][j] = 0 for j >= 1 (a non-empty t cannot be a subsequence of an empty s). Transition: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] (don't use s[i-1] at all — every way of matching t[0..j) inside the shorter prefix s[0..i-1) still works) plus, if s[i-1] == t[j-1], dp[i-1][j-1] (do use s[i-1] to match the last character of t[0..j), reducing to matching t[0..j-1) inside s[0..i-1)). These two branches never overlap (one excludes s[i-1] from the match, the other requires it), so they simply add. The answer is dp[n][m].
